title: Arrival in Fès: sounds, greetings and verb of the Moroccan

blocks.text: The summer of the fifth year Luke passed it to Fès, guest of the family of Karīm al-ʿAlawīThe Commission has already made a number of proposals. This is the opportunity to meet the darija , Arabic spoken in Morocco: the most distant variety from fuṣḥā among those you have encountered, because it reduces many vowels, has loans from Berber (amazigh), French and Spanish, and uses verbal forms that do not exist in Egyptian and Levantine. The MAG track is only understandable: you don't have to speak Moroccan, but understand it enough to follow a simple conversation, recognize the main traits and respond with the courtesy formulas. In this first unit learn sounds, pronouns, possession with dyal, the verb (ka-, n-, ġadi) and denial, with the formulas to greet, thank and stay at the table. Seven weeks, in parallel with B2-18, B2-19 and the beginning of B2-20.

rows: EGY track completed; B2-17 and B2-18 (commutation, passive Levantine)
9–10 hours · seven weeks (weeks 227–233), about 1,5 hours per week in two blocks

blocks.text: Materials This unit, a Moroccan speaker for scripts (tutor or tandem partner), video and Moroccan audio chosen by the tutor
Targets. At the end of the unit you know:
1. recognize the darija and distinguish it from the Egyptian, the Levantine and the fuṣḥā;
2. understanding the typical sounds: reduced vowels, ǧ → ž, ṯ → t, ḏ → d;
3. understand pronouns, possession with dyals and suffixes;
4. understand the verb: present with ka-, the n- of the first person, the future with ġadi, denial but...š and māši;
5. greeting, thanking and responding to table with Moroccan formulas.
Seven-week plan (two blocks from 40–45 minutes per week).

The rhythm. The darija is fast and compact: the short vowels fall, the words shorten (ma-kanfhəmš I don't understand), and often you hear groups of three consonants. The first goal is to recognize root consonants: k-t-b in ktəb, f-h-m kanfhəm.

dyal The possession is often expressed with dyal + suffix, after a name with the article: l-ktab dyali Karīm The mother of Karīm». It's like ⁧بتاع⁩ in Egyptian, but much more frequent. kinship names usually use suffixes: wəldi My son is my son. ḫti My sister, babak, your father.
The verb in comparison.

The n-trap. In Moroccan the prefix n- indicates i , not "noi": nəktəb I'll write it down. kanəktəb I'm writing. The "noi" has n- ... -u: nəktbu, kanəktbu. In Egyptian and fuṣḥā, on the other hand, n- is . It is the most frequent misunderstanding of those who know other dialects. ka- (or ta-). Report current or current: kanšrəb Atay kayḫdəm f-l-bulis is a police officer. In the north and in some cities you can feel ta-: tanəktəb. ġadi. The future: ġadi nəmši I'll go, ġadi yži It will be. Often shortened to ġa-: ġanəmši. bġit. "I want to have the shape of the past: bġit atay \ I want a tea Â Â Â Â Â bġiti? "Do you want to? bġitš I don't want to. Denial. Like Egyptian, but...š around the verb: but kanfhəmš I don't understand, but mšitš I didn't go. In front of names, adjectives and participles is used māši : māši mezyan ... not good... māši daba walu = ... nothing. The interrogative words. šnu / ašnu "What is it?" škun "chi" "fin" where "fin" is "fin" · fuqaš / imta • when • ʿlaš "Why" · kifaš As a result of this test, the following information shall be provided: šḥal "How much " · waš (demand yes/no).
